title: Caffeine: dose, timing and genes
goal: Explain how caffeine works on the brain, work out a dose of 3–6 mg·kg⁻¹, choose timing and form, and judge the evidence on tolerance and CYP1A2 genes.

steps.title: How caffeine works: the brain
steps.text:
During the day [adenosine](g:adenosine) builds up in the brain. It binds its [receptors](g:receptor) and damps down the release of signalling chemicals such as dopamine: you feel tired.

[Caffeine](g:caffeine) has a similar shape. It sits in those receptors and blocks them, so the signalling stays high [[c:caf-adenosine]]. The result: more alertness, stronger drive to the muscles and less pain, so a hard pace feels easier ([RPE](g:rpe) falls) [[c:caf-effects]].

Early theories said caffeine helps by sparing [glycogen](g:glycogen). The brain is now accepted as the main target.

claims.text: Caffeine acts mainly on the brain by blocking adenosine receptors, which raises neurotransmitter release, motor unit firing and pain suppression.

evidence.quote: Caffeine is believed to exert its effects on the CNS via the antagonism of adenosine receptors, leading to increases in neurotransmitter release, motor unit firing rates, and pain suppression
the main target is the CNS, which is now widely accepted as the primary mechanism by which caffeine alters mental and physical performance

claims.text: Caffeine's effects include adenosine receptor antagonism, improved neuromuscular function, vigilance and alertness, and lower perceived exertion.

evidence.quote: Adenosine receptor antagonism; increased endorphin release; improved neuromuscular function; improved vigilance and alertness; reduced the perception of exertion during exercise

steps.title: How much: 3–6 mg·kg⁻¹, and less can work
steps.text:
Caffeine improves performance consistently at **3–6 mg·kg⁻¹** body mass. The smallest dose that works isn't known; it may be as low as 2 mg·kg⁻¹. Very high doses (9 mg·kg⁻¹) aren't needed and often bring side effects such as nausea, anxiety and poor sleep [[c:caf-dose-range]].

Lower doses also work: under 3 mg·kg⁻¹ (about 200 mg), taken before and during exercise with some carbohydrate [[c:caf-low]].

How big is the gain? A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 44 studies found about 2% faster [time trials](g:time-trial) and 3% more mean power, with wide spread between studies [[c:caf-size]]. Endurance is where caffeine helps most consistently, though the size of the gain varies from person to person [[c:caf-endurance]].

claims.text: Caffeine consistently improves performance at 3–6 mg·kg⁻¹; the minimal dose may be about 2 mg·kg⁻¹; 9 mg·kg⁻¹ brings frequent side effects and isn't needed.

evidence.quote: Caffeine has consistently been shown to improve exercise performance when consumed in doses of 3-6 mg/kg body mass. Minimal effective doses of caffeine currently remain unclear but they may be as low as 2 mg/kg body mass. Very high doses of caffeine (e.g. 9 mg/kg) are associated with a high incidence of side-effects and do not seem to be required to elicit an ergogenic effect.
Larger caffeine doses (≥9 mg/kg BM) do not appear to increase the performance benefit,

claims.text: Lower doses (under 3 mg·kg⁻¹, about 200 mg) before and during exercise with carbohydrate are an alternative protocol.

evidence.quote: Lower caffeine doses (<3 mg/kg BM, ~200 mg), provided both before and during exercise; consumed with a CHO source

claims.text: Across 44 studies (corrected analysis), caffeine improved time-trial time by about 2% and mean power by about 3%, with wide variation.

evidence.quote: Caffeine has a small but evident effect on endurance performance when taken in moderate doses (3-6 mg/kg) as well as an overall improvement following caffeine compared to placebo in mean power output (3.03 ± 3.07%; effect size = 0.23 ± 0.15) and time-trial completion time (2.22 ± 2.59%; effect size = 0.41 ± 0.2).

claims.text: Aerobic endurance shows the most consistent moderate-to-large benefits from caffeine, with effects that differ between individuals.

evidence.quote: Aerobic endurance appears to be the form of exercise with the most consistent moderate-to-large benefits from caffeine use, although the magnitude of its effects differs between individuals.

steps.title: Working out a caffeine dose
steps.problem: A 68 kg runner wants 3 mg·kg⁻¹ of caffeine before a 10 km race. How much is that, and how many 100 mg caffeine gels?
steps: Dose = body mass × dose per kg.
Check the top of the range: 6 mg·kg⁻¹ would be 408 mg. Starting low and testing it in training is sensible.

steps.title: When, and in what form
steps.text:
The usual timing is a capsule **about 60 min** before the start. The best timing depends on the form [[c:caf-60]].

Caffeine gum is absorbed faster, through the lining of the mouth, so it needs a shorter wait; total uptake ends up the same [[c:caf-gum]]. Caffeine gum has improved endurance cycling. Mouth rinses with caffeine have mostly shown no benefit in aerobic exercise.

Mind the [half-life](g:half-life): on average 4–6 h, but anything from 1.5 to 10 h in adults [[c:caf-half-life]]. An evening race dose can still be in your blood at bedtime.

claims.text: Caffeine is most often taken 60 min before exercise; optimal timing depends on the source, and gum may need a shorter wait.

evidence.quote: The most commonly used timing of caffeine supplementation is 60 min pre-exercise. Optimal timing of caffeine ingestion likely depends on the source of caffeine. For example, as compared to caffeine capsules, caffeine chewing gums may require a shorter waiting time from consumption to the start of the exercise session.

claims.text: Caffeine gum is absorbed faster through the mouth lining than capsules, with the same total uptake; it improved endurance cycling, while caffeine mouth rinses mostly don't help aerobic exercise.

evidence.quote: Caffeinated chewing gum is absorbed quicker through the buccal mucosa compared with capsule delivery and absorption in the gut, although total caffeine absorption over time is not different.
while the majority of the literature indicates no ergogenic effect on aerobic exercise performance

claims.text: Caffeine's half-life averages 4–6 h but ranges from 1.5 to 10 h in adults.

evidence.quote: While the average half-life (t 1/2 ) of caffeine is generally reported to be between 4 and 6 h, it varies between individuals and even may range from 1.5 to 10 h in adults

steps.title: Does daily coffee blunt the effect?
steps.text:
Many athletes drink coffee every day. Does that blunt the race-day effect? The evidence is mixed [[c:caf-tolerance-mixed]]:

- In 18 people who normally took little caffeine, 4 weeks of daily caffeine built tolerance: the race-day benefit disappeared.
- Another study gave caffeine on 20 days in a row; the benefit stayed, though it shrank.
- 40 trained cyclists were split by daily intake (about 60, 140 and 350 mg). A 6 mg·kg⁻¹ dose improved a ~30 min time trial in all three groups, with no link to habitual intake [[c:caf-habitual]]. But they only went 24 h without caffeine first.

Practical reading: daily coffee probably doesn't cancel the effect, but test it.

claims.text: Four weeks of daily caffeine in low users removed its ergogenic effect in one study; in another, 20 days kept it, though smaller.

evidence.quote: Four weeks of caffeine ingestion resulted in increased tolerance to acute caffeine supplementation in previously low habitual caffeine consumers, with the ergogenic effect of acute caffeine supplementation no longer apparent
These results are in contrast with a recent study in which 20 days of consecutive supplementation with caffeine maintained an ergogenic effect, even though the effect size attenuated over time

claims.text: In 40 trained cyclists, 6 mg·kg⁻¹ caffeine improved time-trial performance regardless of habitual caffeine intake, after only 24 h of withdrawal.

evidence.quote: Caffeine ingestion improved performance as compared to placebo and control, with no influence of habitual caffeine intake.
However, a limitation of this study is the short 24-h caffeine withdrawal period in all groups

debate.question: Does daily caffeine use blunt the performance benefit of a pre-race dose?

sides.position: Yes, it can: 4 weeks of daily caffeine removed the benefit in previously low users.
Not much: in 40 trained cyclists, low, moderate and high habitual users all improved with caffeine.

steps.title: CYP1A2: do your genes decide?
steps.text:
Over 95% of caffeine is broken down in the liver by the enzyme [CYP1A2](g:cyp1a2) [[c:caf-liver]]. A common [polymorphism](g:polymorphism) in its gene gives AA ('fast'), AC or CC ('slow') [genotypes](g:genotype).

In 101 male athletes doing a 10 km cycling time trial, 4 mg·kg⁻¹ made AA riders 6.8% faster, did nothing for AC, and made CC riders 13.7% *slower* [[c:caf-guest2018]]. But a trial in 40 male cyclists found caffeine made a ~30 min time trial faster whatever the genotype [[c:caf-glaister]].

Note: the lead author of the 2018 trial consults for a genetic-testing company [[c:caf-coi]]. Gene tests for caffeine are sold; the evidence doesn't yet support them.

claims.text: Over 95% of caffeine is metabolised in the liver by CYP1A2.

evidence.quote: Over 95% of caffeine is metabolized in the liver by the Cytochrome P450 1A2 (CYP1A2) enzyme

claims.text: In 101 male athletes, 4 mg·kg⁻¹ caffeine improved a 10 km cycling time trial by 6.8% in AA genotypes, had no effect in AC and slowed CC by 13.7%.

evidence.quote: Among those with the AA genotype, cycling time decreased by 4.8% at 2 mg·kg (17.0 ± 0.3 vs 17.8 ± 0.4 min, P = 0.0005) and by 6.8% at 4 mg·kg (16.6 ± 0.3 vs 17.8 ± 0.4 min, P < 0.0001). In those with the CC genotype, 4 mg·kg increased cycling time by 13.7% versus placebo (20.8 ± 0.8 vs 18.3 ± 0.5 min, P = 0.04). No effects were observed among those with the AC genotype.

claims.text: In 40 male cyclists, 5 mg·kg⁻¹ caffeine improved a ~30 min time trial irrespective of ADORA2A or CYP1A2 genotype.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, caffeine influences physiological responses to submaximal exercise and improves time-trial performance irrespective of ADORA2A or CYP1A2 genotypes.

claims.text: The first author of the ISSN caffeine position stand, who led the 2018 genotype trial, consults for a genetic-testing company.

evidence.quote: N.S.G consults for and is on the scientific advisory board of Nutrigenomix, a genetic testing company.

debate.question: Does CYP1A2 genotype decide whether caffeine helps endurance performance?

sides.position: Yes: in 101 athletes, only AA genotypes improved and CC genotypes got slower at 4 mg·kg⁻¹.
No: in 40 cyclists, caffeine improved time-trial performance whatever the CYP1A2 or ADORA2A genotype.

points: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors in the brain: more alertness and drive, less perceived effort.
Dose: 3–6 mg·kg⁻¹ works consistently, possibly from 2 mg·kg⁻¹; 9 mg·kg⁻¹ adds side effects, not speed. Dose = body mass × mg per kg.
Capsules about 60 min before; gum acts faster; the half-life of 4–6 h means evening doses disturb sleep.
Typical gains: about 2% faster time trials. Daily coffee probably doesn't cancel them, but evidence is mixed.
Whether CYP1A2 genotype changes the effect is disputed: test caffeine in training rather than buying a gene test.

variants.stem: Why does a hard pace feel easier after caffeine?

options.text: It blocks adenosine receptors in the brain
options.why: Right: with adenosine blocked, signalling stays high and perceived effort falls.

options.text: It spares muscle glycogen by burning more fat
options.why: An early theory; the brain is now accepted as the main target.

options.text: It supplies extra energy to the muscles
options.why: Caffeine has essentially no energy; it changes signalling.

options.text: It raises VO₂max for a few hours
options.why: The effect is on drive and perceived effort, not on VO₂max.

variants.stem: A 75 kg cyclist wants 3 mg·kg⁻¹ of caffeine before a time trial. How much is that?

options.text: 225 mg
options.why: Right: 75 × 3 = 225 mg.

options.text: 25 mg
options.why: This divides 75 by 3 instead of multiplying.

options.text: 450 mg
options.why: This is 6 mg·kg⁻¹, the top of the range, not 3.
A decimal slip: 10 times the right dose, and a dangerous amount.

variants.solution: Dose = body mass × dose per kg = 75 kg × 3 mg·kg⁻¹ = 225 mg.

variants.stem: A 58 kg triathlete plans 4 mg·kg⁻¹. How many 100 mg caffeine gels is that, closest?

options.text: About 2 gels (232 mg)
options.why: Right: 58 × 4 = 232 mg, a bit over 2 gels.

options.text: About 6 gels (580 mg)
options.why: This takes 10 mg·kg⁻¹, well above the 3–6 range.

options.text: About 1 gel (116 mg)
options.why: This takes 2 mg·kg⁻¹, half the planned dose.

options.text: About 4 gels (400 mg)
options.why: This takes one gel per mg·kg⁻¹: the dose per kg isn't a number of gels. 58 × 4 = 232 mg.

variants.solution: 58 kg × 4 mg·kg⁻¹ = 232 mg; 232 ÷ 100 ≈ 2.3, so about 2 gels.

variants.stem: An 82 kg runner wants the low end, 3 mg·kg⁻¹. How much caffeine?

options.text: 246 mg
options.why: Right: 82 × 3 = 246 mg.

options.text: 27 mg
options.why: This divides 82 by 3.

options.text: 492 mg
options.why: This is 6 mg·kg⁻¹.

options.text: 85 mg
options.why: This adds 82 + 3 instead of multiplying.

variants.stem: A runner reasons: "If 3 mg·kg⁻¹ helps, 9 mg·kg⁻¹ will help three times as much." What does the evidence say?

options.text: No extra benefit, and more side effects
options.why: Right: 9 mg·kg⁻¹ brings frequent nausea, anxiety and poor sleep without a bigger gain.

options.text: Right: the effect rises in step with the dose
options.why: The benefit levels off within 3–6 mg·kg⁻¹.

options.text: 9 mg·kg⁻¹ is needed for endurance events
options.why: Endurance gains are consistent at 3–6 mg·kg⁻¹ and possibly lower.

options.text: Higher doses work, but only in trained runners
options.why: No such split; very high doses aren't needed by anyone.

variants.stem: A triathlete wants a quick caffeine lift for the last part of the run, with little time to wait. Which form acts fastest?

options.text: Caffeine chewing gum
options.why: Right: gum is absorbed through the mouth lining, faster than a swallowed capsule.

options.text: A caffeine capsule
options.why: Capsules are absorbed in the gut, more slowly; the usual wait is about 60 min.

options.text: A caffeine mouth rinse, spat out
options.why: Rinses have mostly shown no benefit in aerobic exercise.

options.text: A strong coffee the night before
options.why: Most of it is gone by morning, and it misses the moment entirely.

variants.stem: A cyclist takes 400 mg of caffeine at 18:00 for a 19:00 criterium and lies awake until 2 am. Best explanation?

options.text: With a 4–6 h half-life, a third to a half remains at midnight
options.why: Right: caffeine is cleared slowly, so an evening dose lingers into the night.

options.text: The race itself, since caffeine is gone within an hour
options.why: Caffeine lasts hours, not one hour.

options.text: Caffeine only disturbs sleep in non-athletes
options.why: Training doesn't remove the effect on sleep.

options.text: The dose was too low to wear off quickly
options.why: A smaller dose leaves less, not more, at bedtime.

variants.stem: A runner drinks four coffees a day and asks whether a caffeine dose before her marathon is pointless. Best answer?

options.text: Probably still helps; the data are mixed, so test it
options.why: Right: in 40 cyclists habitual intake didn't matter, but one study found tolerance after 4 weeks.

options.text: Pointless: daily coffee always cancels the effect
options.why: One study found tolerance, others didn't: 'always' goes too far.

options.text: She must stop all coffee for a month first
options.why: No study shows a month off is needed; 24 h off was used in the cyclist study.

options.text: It works better in heavy coffee drinkers
options.why: No study found a bigger effect in heavy users.

variants.stem: A cyclist is offered a €150 CYP1A2 gene test 'to know if caffeine works for you'. Best advice?

options.text: Skip it: trials disagree; test caffeine in training
options.why: Right: one trial found a gene effect, another found none, so a trial in training tells you more.

options.text: Buy it: CC riders always get slower
options.why: That came from one trial; another found no genotype effect.

options.text: Buy it: AA riders gain 7%, so it predicts your gain
options.why: The 6.8% was a group average in one trial, not a prediction for one person.

options.text: Skip it: CYP1A2 has nothing to do with caffeine
options.why: CYP1A2 breaks down over 95% of caffeine; what's disputed is whether it changes the performance effect.

variants.stem: The 2018 trial found CC riders got slower with caffeine. What most limits that finding?

options.text: One trial, men only; another found no gene effect
options.why: Right: it isn't confirmed, and women weren't tested.

options.text: The dose was far too high to be realistic
options.why: 4 mg·kg⁻¹ sits inside the usual 3–6 range.

options.text: A 10 km time trial is too short to test caffeine
options.why: The riders took about 17–18 min: a typical endurance effort where caffeine helps.

options.text: It had no placebo condition
options.why: It was double-blind and placebo-controlled.
